title: Tech help for seniors in New Jersey: free classes and support
dek: Smartphones, tablets, video calls and patient portals made simpler, plus how to avoid online scams, where to get free tech help across New Jersey and how to lower your internet bill.
keyFacts: New Jerseyans 60+ can take free live online classes through the state's GetSetUp partnership.
Senior Planet's free tech hotline: 888-713-3495, Monday to Saturday, in English, Spanish and Mandarin.
Many NJ libraries offer free one-on-one tech appointments and lend Wi-Fi hotspots.
Federal Lifeline takes up to $9.25 a month off phone or internet service for eligible households.
The ACP internet discount ended June 1, 2024. Sites still offering it may be scams.
body:
Technology has a way of sneaking up on people. The doctor's office wants you on its patient portal. The grandchildren live on video calls. The bank closes a branch and points you to an app. None of this is hard once someone patient shows you how, and in New Jersey a lot of that help is free.

This guide covers the devices and skills that matter most for older adults, how to stay safe online, where to get free tech help in New Jersey, and how to lower the cost of internet service.

Which device should I start with?

Start with what you will actually use. For most people that is one of three things.

  • A smartphone. It goes everywhere and handles calls, texts, photos, video calls and most apps. You can make the text bigger, turn up the volume and use your voice to send messages.
  • A tablet. The bigger screen is easier on the eyes and fingers. Tablets are great for video calls, reading, games and patient portals. Most work on home Wi-Fi only, unless you pay for a data plan.
  • A laptop or desktop computer. Best for typing, filling out long forms, taxes and printing. A larger keyboard and screen help if your hands or eyes give you trouble.

Before you buy, ask a librarian or a tech-savvy friend to show you a couple of models. Many New Jersey libraries also lend devices or Wi-Fi hotspots, so you can try before spending money.

Settings that make life easier

Every phone and tablet has accessibility settings. Ask someone to help you turn on larger text, bolder fonts, louder ring and alert sounds, and captions for videos. Voice assistants can make calls, set reminders and read messages aloud. If you have trouble hearing calls, ask about captioned phone options, and see our hearing aids guide.

What are the most useful things to learn first?

Video calls

A video call lets you see a face, which matters more than people expect. Learn one app well, usually the one your family already uses. Practice with someone you know before a doctor visit or a big family call. Prop the device up at eye level, sit facing a window or lamp, and check that your microphone is not muted.

Patient portals

A patient portal is a secure website or app run by your doctor or hospital. You can see test results, request prescription refills, read visit notes and message your care team. Ask the front desk for an activation code at your next visit.

Medicare also has an online account at Medicare.gov where you can see claims and plan information. Medicare says each account needs its own email address, so do not share one email between spouses. If you need help with Medicare questions, call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) or New Jersey's free SHIP counselors at 1-800-792-8820.

Finding reliable health information

The National Institute on Aging (NIA) suggests starting with federal health sites, such as the National Institutes of Health and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. It advises checking who runs a site, when the information was updated, and being wary of miracle cures. Talk with your doctor before changing anything based on what you read online.

Benefit applications

Many New Jersey programs now have online applications. NJSave, the state's single application for help with Medicare costs, prescriptions and other expenses, can be filed online or on paper. If the online form feels like too much, call 1-800-792-9745 or ask your county office on aging for help. See our guide to PAAD for one of the programs it covers.

How do I stay safe from scams online?

Scammers love technology because it lets them reach thousands of people for free. A few rules stop most of them.

  • Slow down. Scams depend on panic. A message saying your account is locked, a grandchild is in jail or you owe the IRS is a reason to hang up and check.
  • Never pay with gift cards. No real agency or company asks for that. Since October 2025, New Jersey law requires stores that sell gift cards to post a notice warning about gift card scams.
  • Do not click links in unexpected texts or emails. Go to the website yourself or call the number on the back of your card.
  • Never let a stranger take control of your computer, even if they say they are from a well-known tech company.
  • Use strong, different passwords and turn on two-step verification where you can. NIA recommends both.
  • Be careful on public Wi-Fi. NIA suggests not entering sensitive information on public networks.
If you think you've been scammed

Call your bank right away. Then report it to the New Jersey Division of Consumer Affairs at 1-800-242-5846 (toll free in New Jersey) or 973-504-6200, and to the Federal Trade Commission at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Our scams guide walks through the most common schemes and what to do next.

Watch out for websites still advertising the Affordable Connectivity Program (ACP). The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) says that program ended on June 1, 2024, and warns that some sites still collect personal information by claiming to enroll people. If you gave out your Social Security number or bank details to one, visit IdentityTheft.gov.

What do North Jersey families and care professionals say?

In October 2026 we talked with more than 30 private instructors and about 50 older adults, adult children, care managers and home care professionals around North Jersey. Here is what came up most often about technology.

  • Fear of scams is real. Many older adults we spoke with avoid patient portals or online payments because they worry about being hacked. Patient, in-person help builds confidence.
  • The phone still matters. Some people would rather book and pay over the phone. That is a fine choice.
  • An aide or family member often helps. Several people told us their aide or a grown child helps them with the computer. Showing that helper the basics helps too.
  • Comfort is growing. Care managers said far more older adults use tablets and order online than a few years ago, so it is never too late to start.

Where can I get free tech help in New Jersey?

Your public library

Libraries are the best free tech help in the state. Many offer one-on-one appointments with a librarian, group classes on phones and tablets, and loans of hotspots or devices. A few real examples:

  • The Middletown Township Public Library in Monmouth County offers one-on-one technology training with a librarian, up to an hour per appointment and one appointment a month. Request it through the library's online form at least three days ahead.
  • The Cherry Hill Public Library in Camden County offers one-hour librarian tech appointments, regular computer classes and mobile hotspots that cardholders can borrow for seven days.
  • The Somerset County Library System has brought its traveling library to the county's Senior Wellness Centers, where staff help with library cards and technology questions.

The New Jersey State Library also funds digital skills programs. In December 2025 it awarded nearly $109,000 in Expanding Digital Literacy grants to five public libraries, with older adults among the groups the projects aim to reach. Its list shows 96 New Jersey libraries using Northstar Digital Literacy, a self-guided online tool that teaches basics like email, internet use and telehealth appointments.

If your vision is changing

LEAP, the Library Equal Access Program, gives free computer and iPad training to New Jersey residents 55 and older who have had a change in vision. It is run with the New Jersey Commission for the Blind and Visually Impaired. Contact the Talking Book and Braille Center at 800-792-8322, ext. 812.

Free online classes for New Jerseyans 60 and up

The New Jersey Department of Human Services partners with GetSetUp to offer free live online classes for residents 60 and older. Classes are taught by peers, and there are more than 500 to choose from, including iPad and Chromebook basics, using voice assistants and understanding the cloud. There are even New Jersey only sessions on filling out the NJSave application. GetSetUp's support line is 888-559-1614.

Senior Planet from AARP

Senior Planet, a nonprofit affiliate of AARP, runs free online technology classes and a free tech hotline at 888-713-3495. Specialists answer Monday through Saturday in English, Spanish and Mandarin. If you need more help, they can set up a free one-on-one video session with a volunteer.

Senior centers and county offices

Some senior centers host tech help days, sometimes with library staff or student volunteers. Ask your county office on aging what runs near you. Call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737, or dial 2-1-1.

How can I lower the cost of internet and phone service?

The federal Lifeline program gives a discount of up to $9.25 a month on phone, internet or bundled service for eligible low-income households. Only one Lifeline benefit is allowed per household. You qualify if your household income is at or below 135% of the federal poverty guidelines, or if someone in your household gets SNAP, Medicaid (NJ FamilyCare), SSI, federal public housing assistance or a veterans pension.

  1. Check eligibility. Apply online through the FCC's National Verifier at lifelinesupport.org, by mail, or through a participating phone or internet company.
  2. Pick a provider. Choose a company in your area that participates in Lifeline and ask it to apply the discount.
  3. Recertify every year. If you do not, you will be dropped.

For help or a paper form, call the Lifeline support center at 1-800-234-9473. Do not confuse this federal discount with New Jersey's Lifeline Utility Assistance, a separate $225 a year utility benefit for people who qualify for PAAD. See our food and utility help guide for that one.

Many internet companies also run their own low-cost plans for households on SNAP, Medicaid or SSI. Call your provider and ask what it offers for low-income or older customers. Get the price, speed and any equipment fees in writing, and ask what happens when a promotional rate ends.

Public Wi-Fi at libraries, and hotspots you can borrow, can bridge the gap if home internet is out of reach.

What about private help at home?

Sometimes the easiest answer is a patient person sitting beside you at your own kitchen table. Some people hire a tech tutor who comes to the house. A good one can set up a new phone, organize photos, teach video calls or connect a printer.

Before you hire anyone, ask for references, the hourly rate and whether they carry insurance. Never give a helper your passwords to keep, and watch what they do on your accounts. A good tutor teaches you to do it yourself. If a family member helps instead, ask them to write each step on an index card you can keep by the device.

The goal is confidence. One skill at a time, practiced until it feels ordinary.

Technology is one of the easiest ways to stay in touch. For more on that, read our guide to staying connected in New Jersey, and for classes of every kind, see learning something new.

faq.q: Where can I get free help with my smartphone in New Jersey?
faq.a: Start with your public library. Many offer one-on-one appointments and classes. You can also call Senior Planet's free hotline at 888-713-3495 or take free online classes through GetSetUp if you are a New Jersey resident 60 or older.

faq.q: Is the Affordable Connectivity Program still available?
faq.a: No. The FCC says the ACP discount ended on June 1, 2024. Be careful of websites that still claim to enroll people, since some collect personal information.

faq.q: Who qualifies for the Lifeline phone and internet discount?
faq.a: Households with income at or below 135% of the federal poverty guidelines, or where someone gets SNAP, Medicaid, SSI, federal public housing assistance or a veterans pension. The discount is up to $9.25 a month, one per household.

faq.q: What is a patient portal and how do I sign up?
faq.a: It is a secure website or app from your doctor or hospital where you can see test results, request refills and message your care team. Ask the front desk for an activation code at your next visit.

faq.q: What should I do if I think I was scammed online?
faq.a: Call your bank first. Then report it to the New Jersey Division of Consumer Affairs at 1-800-242-5846 or 973-504-6200, and to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

faq.q: Is there tech help for people with low vision?
faq.a: Yes. LEAP, the Library Equal Access Program, offers free computer and iPad training to New Jersey residents 55 and older with a change in vision. Call the Talking Book and Braille Center at 800-792-8322, ext. 812.

faq.q: How can I help my parent get comfortable with a smartphone or tablet?
faq.a: Pick one or two things that matter to them, like video calls with grandchildren, and practice those first. Free help is available at many New Jersey libraries and senior centers, and a patient helper who comes to the home can make a big difference.

title: Volunteering after 60 in New Jersey: where to start
dek: AmeriCorps Seniors, AARP Tax-Aide, Medicare counseling, nursing home advocacy, food banks and more: the New Jersey volunteer programs that welcome older adults, how to choose one and how to get there without a car.
keyFacts: AmeriCorps Seniors programs take volunteers 55 and older. Some offer a small tax-free stipend to income-eligible volunteers.
AARP Foundation Tax-Aide trains volunteers with no tax background. Tax season runs February through mid-April.
Nursing home volunteer advocates get 36 hours of free virtual training and visit at least 4 hours a week.
Ask about volunteering as a SHIP Medicare counselor at 1-800-792-8820.
Find opportunities statewide at volunteernewjersey.org.
body:
New Jersey has plenty of volunteer work built for people over 60. AmeriCorps Seniors programs take volunteers 55 and older, and some pay a small tax-free stipend to volunteers with lower incomes. AARP Foundation Tax-Aide trains volunteers to do free tax returns. The state's Medicare counseling program and its nursing home ombudsman both train older adults to help their peers. Food banks, libraries and hospitals need regular hands too.

The best fit depends on what you want from it. Some people want a team and a fixed schedule. Some want to use a skill from their working life. Some just want a reason to get dressed on Tuesday. This guide covers the main programs, how to choose, and how to get there if you no longer drive.

Why volunteer after 60?

Volunteering gives you a purpose, a group of people who expect you and something to look forward to every week. For many older adults, that weekly anchor matters more than the task itself.

AmeriCorps says 84 percent of its AmeriCorps Seniors volunteers report stable or improving health after one year of service, and that 88 percent of volunteers who felt a lack of companionship felt less isolated after joining. Those are the program's own figures. Retirement, the loss of a spouse or giving up the car can shrink a person's world quickly. A standing commitment pushes back against that.

You will have company. In the 2023 civic engagement survey run by AmeriCorps and the U.S. Census Bureau, 25.7 percent of New Jersey residents volunteered through an organization, according to the state Department of State.

The most useful volunteer job is the one you will still be showing up for in six months.

What is AmeriCorps Seniors, and is it in New Jersey?

AmeriCorps Seniors is the federal volunteer network for people 55 and older. It has three main programs, and New Jersey has local sponsors for each. Availability depends on where you live, since each program covers certain counties.

RSVP

RSVP matches volunteers with local nonprofits based on their interests. AmeriCorps says commitments range from a few hours to 40 hours a week. AmeriCorps says most AmeriCorps Seniors programs offer accident, personal liability and excess auto liability insurance.

In Gloucester County, AmeriCorps Seniors RSVP is run through Rowan College of South Jersey in West Deptford. Membership is free. Volunteers serve an average of three or four hours a week at local agencies, and the office also offers SHIP Medicare counseling and a Friendly Caller and Visitor program for homebound neighbors. Volunteers who visit homes are background checked, trained and fingerprinted. Call 856-468-1742.

Foster Grandparents

Foster Grandparents mentor and tutor children. New Jersey's Department of State says the focus here is school readiness and kindergarten through 12th grade, with volunteers working hands-on in classrooms on reading, basic math and social skills. No teaching background is needed.

In South Jersey, Gateway Community Action Partnership runs a Foster Grandparent Program serving Atlantic, Burlington, Camden, Gloucester and Salem counties, in Head Start and Early Head Start classrooms, schools and community settings. Volunteers generally serve at least 15 hours a week. Eligible volunteers can receive a tax-free hourly stipend and transportation help or reimbursement. Call 609-487-4569.

Senior Companions

Senior Companions visit older adults who need help to keep living at home, offering friendship and help with everyday tasks such as shopping or paying bills. They also give family caregivers a break. In Union County, Jewish Family Service of Central New Jersey in Elizabeth runs an AmeriCorps Senior Companion program through its Friendly Visitor Program. Volunteers 55 and older who qualify can receive a stipend. Call 908-352-8375.

To search for other programs near you, use the AmeriCorps Seniors Pathfinder on AmeriCorps.gov or call AmeriCorps at 1-800-942-2677. Programs and the counties they cover change, so call before you plan around one.

Can I use my work skills as a volunteer?

Yes. Three statewide programs train older adults to help their neighbors with money, health insurance and nursing home problems. Each comes with real training and a clear role.

AARP Foundation Tax-Aide

Tax-Aide volunteers prepare free tax returns, mostly for older adults with low incomes. You do not need a tax background; AARP provides the training. Tax counselors prepare returns. Client facilitators greet people and organize paperwork. Technology specialists look after the computers, and bilingual volunteers are in high demand. AARP says volunteers serve one to three days a week during tax season, which runs February through mid-April. Sites recruit and train ahead of the season, so apply early through AARP's Tax-Aide volunteer page. If you need tax help yourself, see free tax help for seniors in NJ.

SHIP Medicare counselors

New Jersey's State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) gives free, unbiased Medicare counseling through a network of more than 300 trained counselors in all 21 counties. Counselors do not sell or recommend any plan. If you understand Medicare, or are willing to learn, call 1-800-792-8820 to ask about volunteering. Appointments are held in person, by phone and virtually, which suits volunteers who do not drive.

Long-Term Care Ombudsman volunteer advocates

Certified Volunteer Advocates visit nursing homes to help residents solve problems and make sure they are treated with dignity. The state Office of the Long-Term Care Ombudsman gives 36 hours of virtual training and a certification exam. New advocates then work alongside an experienced volunteer for about two weeks before being assigned to a nursing home close to home. You set your own hours but must visit at least four hours a week. The office says it has about 150 advocates and needs many more. Details and regional contacts are on the ombudsman's volunteer page, or call 1-877-582-6995. If a family member is choosing a home, see how to read nursing home ratings.

Where else can I volunteer in New Jersey?

Food banks, libraries, hospitals and senior programs all rely on volunteers. Most will tell you on the first call what training, checks or health forms they need.

  • Food banks. The Community FoodBank of New Jersey takes volunteers at its Hillside, Egg Harbor Township and Garfield locations. You must sign up in advance online (no walk-ins), wear closed-toe shoes and dress for a warehouse that is not temperature controlled. Tasks include sorting and repacking food and building senior food boxes. Other regional food banks and local church and synagogue pantries need help too.
  • Meals on Wheels. Drivers and packers are always needed, and a delivery route gives you a quick check-in with neighbors who live alone. See Meals on Wheels in NJ for your county's program.
  • Libraries. Ask about shelving, book sales run by the Friends of the Library, adult literacy tutoring and helping at programs.
  • Hospitals. Many hospitals have a volunteer office. Roles include information desks, gift shops and patient escort. Expect an application and some health screening. Requirements vary by hospital.
  • Senior centers. Teach a class you know, lead a walking group or help at lunch. See our senior center guide.
  • Phone-based roles. Telephone reassurance programs train volunteers to call older adults who live alone. Our guide to staying connected lists some.

For one place to browse, the state points residents to Volunteer New Jersey, its statewide site for finding opportunities near you.

How do I choose the right volunteer role?

Match the role to the schedule you can keep, the people you want to be around and how physical you want it to be. Try one before committing to two.

  1. Pick a who. Children, older adults, animals, patients or the public. People usually stay longest when they like who they are helping.
  2. Pick a rhythm. A weekly shift builds friendships. A seasonal role like Tax-Aide fits people who travel in summer or winter.
  3. Be honest about your body. Warehouse shifts mean standing and lifting. Desk, phone and tutoring roles are easier on knees and backs.
  4. Ask about training and support. Good programs tell you who to call when something goes wrong.
  5. Ask about money. Find out whether there is a stipend, mileage reimbursement or insurance. AmeriCorps stipends are for income-eligible volunteers only.
  6. Give it a month. The first few shifts can feel awkward. That usually passes once people know your name.

If you want paid part-time work instead, see working after 60 in New Jersey.

How can I get there if I don't drive?

Choose a role near transit, ask the program about transportation help, or volunteer from home by phone or computer. Giving up the car does not have to mean giving up the commitment.

  • NJ Transit. Riders 62 and older get reduced fares. See how to get NJ Transit reduced fares.
  • County senior transportation. Many counties run rides for older adults. Call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 to reach your county office on aging and ask whether volunteer trips qualify.
  • Ask the program. Some, like Gateway's Foster Grandparent Program, offer transportation help to eligible volunteers.
  • Go with a friend. Signing up in pairs solves the ride problem and makes the first day easier.
  • Stay home. Phone reassurance calls and SHIP phone counseling can be done from the kitchen table.

More options are in when a parent stops driving.

For adult children

If your mom or dad has gone quiet since retiring or losing a spouse, a volunteer role can be easier to suggest than "you should get out more." Offer to make the first call with them, drive to the first shift, or sign up together for a one-time event.

faq.q: What volunteer programs are there for seniors in New Jersey?
faq.a: AmeriCorps Seniors programs (RSVP, Foster Grandparents and Senior Companions) take volunteers 55 and older. AARP Foundation Tax-Aide, the SHIP Medicare counseling program and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman's volunteer advocate program also train older adults. Food banks, libraries, hospitals and Meals on Wheels need volunteers too.

faq.a: Volunteers are not paid wages. Some AmeriCorps Seniors programs, such as Foster Grandparents and Senior Companions, offer a modest tax-free stipend to income-eligible volunteers, and some offer transportation help. Ask each program about its rules.

faq.q: How do I help my mom find volunteer work after my dad died?
faq.a: Start with what she enjoys and how often she wants to go out. Call her senior center or the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 for local options, then offer to make the first call with her or go to the first shift together. A weekly role with the same people tends to stick.

faq.a: Look for roles near NJ Transit (riders 62 and older get reduced fares), ask the county office on aging about senior rides, ask the program about transportation help, or choose phone-based work such as telephone reassurance calls or SHIP Medicare counseling.

faq.q: How old do you have to be for AmeriCorps Seniors?
faq.a: You must be 55 or older. Use the AmeriCorps Seniors Pathfinder on AmeriCorps.gov to find programs near you, or call AmeriCorps at 1-800-942-2677.

faq.a: New Jersey's Certified Volunteer Advocates complete 36 hours of virtual training and a certification exam, then visit an assigned nursing home for at least four hours a week. Call the Long-Term Care Ombudsman at 1-877-582-6995.

title: Senior discounts in New Jersey: what starts at 62, 65 and 70
dek: The best senior discounts in New Jersey come from the state and federal government. Here they are by age, with what each saves and how to claim it.
keyFacts: 62+: free lifetime NJ State Park pass and $2 off state campsites
62+: half-price NJ Transit fares and the $80 lifetime federal Senior Pass
65+: PATH fare $1.60, Amtrak 10% off, $7 off car registration
65+: extra $1,000 NJ income tax exemption
70+: no freshwater fishing license needed for NJ residents
body:
The best senior discounts in New Jersey come from the state and federal government. At 62, residents get a free lifetime State Park pass, half-price NJ Transit fares and can buy the federal $80 lifetime Senior Pass for national parks. At 65 come cheaper PATH rides ($1.60), $7 off car registration, an extra $1,000 state income tax exemption and lower hunting and fishing licenses. At 70, freshwater fishing is free.

Many of these never show up on a receipt, so people miss them for years. This guide sorts the verified ones by the age they start, says what to bring, and flags the ones tied to income. For fun things to do with your new passes, our list of free and discounted things to do after 60 has museums, college classes and county parks.

What senior discounts start at each age in New Jersey?

Most public discounts start at 62 or 65. A few, like free freshwater fishing, start at 70. Here is the short version, with details below.

AgeDiscountSaves
62NJ State Park senior passFree entry and parking
62State park campsites$2 off per night
62NJ Transit senior fareHalf the one-way fare
62Federal Senior Pass$80 lifetime, $20 a year
65PATH reduced fare$1.60 a ride, not $3.25
65Amtrak10% on most fares
65Car registration$7 less a year
65NJ income taxExtra $1,000 exemption
65Hunting and fishingSenior license prices
70Freshwater fishingNo license needed

Figures checked on official sites in November 2026. Prices can change, so confirm before you buy.

Which discounts start at 62?

Four big ones: the free State Park pass, cheaper state campsites, NJ Transit's senior fare and the federal America the Beautiful Senior Pass.

The New Jersey State Park Senior Citizen Pass

New Jersey residents 62 or older get free admission and free parking at state parks, forests and recreation areas that charge fees. The pass is free and good for life. Apply at any park office or by mail with the state's application form, along with proof of age and residency. For questions, call the Division of Parks and Forestry at 1-800-843-6420.

This matters most in summer. From Memorial Day weekend to Labor Day, popular parks charge daily fees, up to $10 for a resident car on weekends at places like Island Beach, High Point and Round Valley. Island Beach also charges $5 a day the rest of the year. The same senior pass takes $2 a night off state park campsite fees. Residents who are totally disabled qualify too, at any age.

NJ Transit's senior fare

Riders 62 and older pay half the regular one-way fare on NJ Transit buses, trains and light rail. You do not need to sign up. A Medicare card, driver's license or other government ID with your birth date is enough. Our NJ Transit senior fare guide covers which tickets to buy and the free Reduced Fare card.

The federal Senior Pass

U.S. citizens and residents 62 or older can buy the America the Beautiful Senior Pass. The lifetime version costs $80. The annual version costs $20 and can be upgraded in person later. It covers entrance and standard day-use fees at national parks and other federal sites, and gives the passholder a discount on some extras such as camping. Buy it in person at a federal site, as a digital pass on Recreation.gov, or by mail through the USGS store, which can take up to three weeks. Lost passes are not replaced. Older Golden Age Passports still work.

One free trip to a state park office at 62 pays off every summer for the rest of your life.

Which discounts start at 65?

At 65 you add PATH and Amtrak discounts, a smaller car registration bill, a bigger state tax exemption and cheaper hunting and fishing licenses.

PATH

PATH riders 65 and older pay $1.60 one way instead of $3.25. You apply once for a TAPP Reduced Fare Card. Once approved, you can use that card or link your own contactless card or phone to the senior fare. PATH stopped taking SmartLink cards and MetroCards on September 1, 2026, so an old senior SmartLink no longer works. The deadline to ask for a SmartLink balance transfer to TAPP is February 2027. Call PATH at 1-800-234-7284 for help.

Amtrak

Travelers 65 and older get 10% off most Amtrak rail fares. Choose "Senior" as the traveler type when booking. The discount does not apply to sleeping car charges and may not combine with other deals. Bring proof of age on the train.

Car registration

The Motor Vehicle Commission charges owners 65 and older $7 less than the regular passenger vehicle registration fee. People in PAAD, SSI or the state's Lifeline utility program get a reduced registration fee at any age. Bring your current PAAD card, SSI card or proof of Lifeline, in the name of the vehicle owner. If your parent stops driving, our guide to when a parent stops driving covers turning in plates and getting a non-driver ID.

State income tax

New Jersey gives an extra $1,000 exemption to anyone 65 or older on the last day of the tax year, and another $1,000 for a spouse who is also 65. Many people 62 and older can also exclude much of their pension and retirement income. Our guide to how New Jersey taxes retirement income explains the exclusion and its income limits.

Hunting and fishing licenses

Resident licenseRegular65 and older
Freshwater fishing$22.50$12.50 (65 to 69)
Firearm hunting$27.50$15.50
Bow and arrow$31.50$16.50

At 70, New Jersey residents need no freshwater fishing license and no trout stamp. A driver's license or other proof of age serves as the license, and all fishing rules still apply. Our senior fishing guide covers saltwater registration and places with railings and docks. For licensing help, call NJ Fish and Wildlife at 609-292-2965.

Which discounts depend on income, not age?

The biggest savings for many older adults come from income-based programs. They are worth far more than a 10% discount at a store.

  • Prescriptions. PAAD cuts copays to $5 for generics and $7 for brand-name drugs for people 65 and older under its income limits. Call 1-800-792-9745.
  • Utility bills. The state's Lifeline program pays $225 a year toward utilities, with the same income rules as PAAD. LIHEAP and the Universal Service Fund help with heating and electric bills.
  • Phone or internet. The federal Lifeline program takes up to $9.25 a month off internet or bundled service, or up to $5.25 off phone-only service. You qualify through SNAP, Medicaid, SSI, federal public housing aid or a veterans pension, or with income at or below 135% of the poverty guidelines. Call 1-800-234-9473.
  • Museums and the arts. SNAP households can use the Families First Discovery Pass for free or reduced admission at participating New Jersey arts and history groups. Show the Families First EBT card. Each place sets its own discount. See our SNAP for seniors guide to apply.
  • Property taxes. ANCHOR, Senior Freeze and Stay NJ are covered in our property tax relief guide. Homeowners with very low incomes may also get the $250 senior deduction.

Do museums and theaters give senior discounts?

Many do, but the age and price vary, so check each place's own website before you go. Ask for the senior price at the ticket desk even if it is not posted.

Here is one example of how it works. The Newark Museum of Art charges $10 for adults and $8 for seniors 65 and older. Newark residents and veterans get in free, and so do Families First Discovery Pass holders. Many libraries also lend free museum passes. County golf courses and theaters often post senior rates too, so ask before you pay.

How do I make sure my parent is getting these?

Most of these take one trip, one form or one phone call. A free afternoon can set up years of savings.

  1. Gather ID. Put the driver's license or non-driver ID and the Medicare card in one place. Together they prove age and New Jersey residency for nearly everything here.
  2. Get the State Park pass. Stop at any state park office, or mail the application. Keep the pass in the car.
  3. Check the car registration. At the next renewal, make sure the senior rate, or the PAAD, SSI or Lifeline rate, is applied.
  4. Check last year's tax return. Confirm the $1,000 senior exemption and any retirement income exclusion were claimed. Free tax preparation for older adults starts each winter through AARP Tax-Aide and VITA.
  5. Screen for the income programs. Call your county office on aging through the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 and ask about PAAD, Lifeline, SNAP and energy help.
  6. Set up transit. If your parent rides PATH, apply for the TAPP Reduced Fare Card now that old cards no longer work.
Watch out for "senior discount" calls

Real discounts rarely come by phone. Be wary of anyone who calls offering a senior discount you never asked about, especially if they want a card number or Medicare number. That is a common opening for a scam. Our scams guide explains what to do.

faq.q: What discounts do seniors get in New Jersey at 62?
faq.a: A free lifetime State Park pass with free entry and parking, $2 off state park campsites, half-price NJ Transit fares, and the option to buy the federal America the Beautiful Senior Pass for $80 for life or $20 a year.

faq.q: How do I get a State Park senior pass for my mom?
faq.a: She needs to be a New Jersey resident 62 or older. Bring her ID showing age and New Jersey address to any state park office, or mail the state's application. Call 1-800-843-6420 with questions.

faq.q: Is there a senior discount on car registration in NJ?
faq.a: Yes. Owners 65 and older pay $7 less than the regular passenger vehicle registration fee. People in PAAD, SSI or the Lifeline utility program get a reduced fee at any age if they show their card or proof.

faq.q: How much is PATH for seniors?
faq.a: Riders 65 and older pay $1.60 one way, compared with $3.25. Apply for a TAPP Reduced Fare Card. SmartLink cards and MetroCards stopped working on PATH on September 1, 2026.

faq.q: Do seniors need a fishing license in New Jersey?
faq.a: Residents 70 and older need no freshwater fishing license or trout stamp. Residents 65 to 69 pay $12.50 for a senior license. Anglers 16 and older must still register for free to fish in salt water.

faq.q: How can I tell if my dad is missing discounts?
faq.a: Check his car registration and last state tax return for the senior rate and $1,000 exemption, get him the free State Park pass, and call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 to screen for PAAD, Lifeline and SNAP.

title: Access Link and county paratransit in New Jersey
dek: Who qualifies for NJ Transit's Access Link, how to apply, what it costs, the booking and no-show rules, and how county senior transportation differs.
keyFacts: Access Link serves riders who cannot use the local bus due to a disability
Service area: within 3/4 mile of local bus or light rail routes
Book 1 to 7 days ahead; no same-day rides
Approved riders are automatically eligible for NJ Transit reduced fares
Apply: 973-491-4224, option 1
body:
Access Link is NJ Transit's shared-ride van and sedan service for people whose disability keeps them from using the local bus or light rail. It picks up and drops off within three quarters of a mile of a regular local bus or light rail route, during the same days and hours those routes run. Riders must be approved first through an interview and a doctor's verification. The fare is based on the local bus fare.

County paratransit is a separate service. Every New Jersey county runs one for older residents and people with disabilities, so your parent may qualify by age alone. If your mom or dad is slowing down but still sharp, the county service is often the easier first call. If a disability makes the bus impossible, Access Link adds rides for any purpose.

What is Access Link?

Access Link is NJ Transit's paratransit program under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). It is public transportation, run like the bus, for people who cannot ride the bus.

A few things make it different from a taxi. It is shared, so other riders may be picked up or dropped off on the way. It is curb to curb. Drivers help riders board, secure wheelchairs and get off, but they do not carry packages. Help beyond the curb is decided case by case and has to be requested ahead. NJ Transit says the ride time should be comparable to the same trip on the local bus, counting the wait and the walk to and from the stops.

There are no limits on trip purpose. NJ Transit lists work, school, shopping, social visits, doctors, dentists, errands, or "just to get out of the house and relax." Trips are not ranked, so a hair appointment counts the same as a checkup.

If there is no local bus near your parent's home, there is no Access Link either.

Who qualifies for Access Link?

People with a disability that prevents them from using NJ Transit's local bus or light rail for some or all trips. Age alone does not qualify anyone.

Under the ADA, the disability must affect a major life function, such as walking, seeing, hearing, breathing, thinking or communicating. The question is whether your parent can get to the stop, wait, board and ride safely. A father with advanced Parkinson's who cannot stand at a bus stop may qualify. A mother who simply prefers not to ride the bus would not.

Visitors count too. If your parent already has paratransit eligibility in another state, NJ Transit will honor it for 21 days within a 365-day period after a short application. That helps when grandparents come for the holidays.

How do I apply for my mom or dad?

Call Access Link at 973-491-4224 and choose option 1 for the Certification group. Staff explain the choices and schedule an eligibility interview if it makes sense.

  1. Call option 1. Certification takes calls Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., except holidays. You can call on your parent's behalf.
  2. Do the interview. It is by phone or in person with one of NJ Transit's community partners. Your parent will be asked how and when the disability keeps them from riding the bus.
  3. Send medical verification. NJ Transit requires current verification of the disability. Ask the doctor's office early, because forms often sit for days.
  4. Wait for the letter. NJ Transit says decisions are sent within 21 calendar days of a complete assessment. If it runs late, your parent gets presumptive eligibility and can book rides until a decision is made.
  5. Keep the letter. The last page proves eligibility when traveling to another state.

Once approved, your parent gets a customer ID number and a four-digit PIN for booking. Expect to be asked to recertify from time to time. NJ Transit says riders who do not take part may have their ID deactivated until the information comes in.

Where does Access Link go, and how much does it cost?

It goes anywhere within the Access Link service area, which follows NJ Transit's local bus and light rail routes, not commuter bus routes. The fare is based on the local bus fare, the number of zones and any transfers.

QuestionAccess Link answer
AreaWithin 3/4 mile of local bus or light rail
HoursSame as local bus, weekends and holidays included
FareBased on local bus fare and zones
PaymentEZ-Wallet account or exact cash
HelperApproved care attendant rides free
CompanionPays the same fare as the rider

The Reduced Fare card does not work on Access Link itself. But under a 2020 state law, anyone NJ Transit approves for Access Link is automatically eligible for the Reduced Fare Program, which cuts regular bus, train and light rail fares roughly in half. Riders 62 and older already get senior fares. Our guide to NJ Transit reduced fares explains the ID to carry.

Access Link does not currently run in Sussex, Warren or Hunterdon counties. In those counties, the county service is the place to start.

Service area lines can move. If NJ Transit changes a bus route, some addresses may fall outside the area. When an address is outside, the reservationist will suggest a nearby corner inside it.

How do I book a ride, and what are the rules?

Book 1 to 7 days ahead by phone, online at accesslink.njtransit.com, or in the Access Link app. There are no same-day rides.

  • Phone. Option 2. Next-day rides are booked daily from 7:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Rides further out are booked until 3 p.m.
  • Online or app. NJ Transit's guidelines say next-day rides can be booked until 5 p.m. the day before, and rides 2 to 7 days out at any hour.
  • Have ready. ID and PIN, full addresses with cross streets, the pickup time, a cell number, and whether a care attendant, companion, wheelchair or walker is coming.
  • Pickup window. ADA rules let pickups fall within an hour either side of the requested time. A pilot lets riders ask for a drop-off time instead, for important appointments. Ask about it when you book.
  • Five minutes. Once the vehicle arrives, the driver waits five minutes.
  • Standing rides. For trips at the same time every week, ask for a subscription. Subscriptions are canceled automatically on major holidays.

NJ Transit has held a public hearing on a proposal to change the advance reservation window, so confirm the current rule when you call.

Canceling and no-shows

This is where many families get tripped up. Cancel at least two hours before the pickup window. Canceling between two hours and 50 minutes ahead is a late cancellation (half a point). Less than 50 minutes is a "no-show in transit" (one point). Missing the van or canceling after it arrives is a no-show (two points). Riders who book at least 10 rides in a month and reach infraction points equal to 20% or more of those rides can face suspensions starting at a warning, then 7, 14, 21 and 30 days. Suspensions can be appealed.

Access Link: 973-491-4224

Option 1 to apply. Option 2 to book. Option 3 to cancel and option 4 for ride status, both 5 a.m. to 10 p.m. daily. Option 5 for customer service and help beyond curb to curb. TT users can call 800-955-6765.

How is county paratransit different?

County services serve older residents as well as people with disabilities. Rules, fares, hours and how far they travel vary a lot, so call your county.

The Division of Disability Services says each of New Jersey's 21 counties provides paratransit for older residents and people with disabilities. NJ Transit says many community services are funded through federal transit grants and state Casino Revenue Fund money under the Senior Citizens and Disabled Residents Transportation Assistance Program. Some are open to the public. Others are limited to older adults, people with disabilities or social service clients.

Unlike Access Link, county services are not tied to bus routes, and NJ Transit says community services may run curb to curb, door to door or by advance reservation. Many ask for several days' notice and some limit trip types, so ask. A few North Jersey numbers listed by both the state and NJ Transit:

  • Bergen County Transportation: 201-368-5955
  • Morris County MAPS and Dial-a-Ride: 973-829-8103
  • Passaic County Paratransit: 973-305-5756
  • Hudson County TRANSCEND: 201-369-4320

Every county's number is on our guide to rides to medical appointments, and your county page lists senior centers, which often run town vans too. Our guide to senior bus trips covers day outings.

What else helps when a parent stops driving?

Use both services together, and consider travel training if your parent could still manage the bus with some coaching.

The New Jersey Travel Independence Program (NJTIP) at Rutgers teaches older adults and people with disabilities to ride buses and trains safely. The only cost during training is the rider's own fares, and NJ Transit says each graduate receives a free one-month bus pass. Call 848-932-4499.

If your parent has NJ FamilyCare, rides to covered medical care are free through Modivcare at 1-866-527-9933, booked two days ahead. For a bigger picture of life after the keys, read when a parent stops driving and getting a non-driver ID. A parking placard helps on days a family member drives.

faq.q: How do I sign my mom up for Access Link?
faq.a: Call 973-491-4224 and choose option 1, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. NJ Transit will schedule a phone or in-person interview and ask for current medical verification of her disability. Decisions are sent within 21 calendar days of a complete assessment.

faq.q: Is my dad eligible for Access Link just because he is over 65?
faq.a: No. Access Link is for people whose disability keeps them from using the local bus or light rail. For age-based rides, call your county paratransit service, which serves older residents as well as people with disabilities.

faq.q: How much does Access Link cost?
faq.a: It is not free. The fare is based on the local bus fare, the zones traveled and any transfers. An approved personal care attendant rides free. The Reduced Fare card cannot be used on Access Link.

faq.q: Can I book an Access Link ride for today?
faq.a: No. Access Link does not offer same-day reservations. Book 1 to 7 days ahead by phone, online at accesslink.njtransit.com or in the app.

faq.q: What happens if my parent misses an Access Link pickup?
faq.a: It counts as a no-show. The driver waits five minutes after arriving. Repeated no-shows and late cancellations can lead to suspensions, which can be appealed through customer service at 973-491-4224, option 5.

faq.q: Does Access Link go to my parent's house in a rural area?
faq.a: Only if the address is within three quarters of a mile of a local NJ Transit bus or light rail route. If not, call your county paratransit service, which often covers areas without bus lines.

title: Pets and older adults in New Jersey: costs, help and planning
dek: The health upsides and fall risks of pets, New Jersey's $10 spay and neuter program, pet rights in senior housing, and how to plan for a pet's care.
keyFacts: NJ spays or neuters pets for $10 for owners on PAAD, SSI, Medicaid, SNAP or Lifeline
NJ law lets residents 62+ in senior housing projects keep a pet after written notice
Dogs 7 months and older need a yearly town license and rabies shot
NJ recognizes pet trusts (N.J.S.A. 3B:11-38)
CDC: fracture rates from pet-related falls are highest at 75+
body:
For many older adults a dog or cat is company, routine and a reason to get up in the morning. Research summarized by the National Institutes of Health has found that time with animals can lower stress hormones and blood pressure and ease loneliness, though results are mixed. Pets also bring costs, chores and a real fall risk, so a little planning helps your mom or dad keep one safely.

New Jersey offers some practical help. A state program spays or neuters a dog or cat for $10 if the owner gets benefits such as PAAD, SSI, Medicaid, SNAP or Lifeline. A state law lets residents 62 and older in senior housing projects keep a pet after giving written notice. And New Jersey law recognizes trusts that pay for a pet's care after the owner dies.

Are pets good for older adults' health?

They can be. NIH says interacting with animals has been shown to lower cortisol and blood pressure, and other studies found animals can reduce loneliness, increase feelings of social support and boost mood. NIH also says the research is still young and results have been mixed.

The benefit depends on the person and the pet. An NIH researcher put it simply. If the goal is more activity, a dog that needs walks several times a day helps. If the goal is calm, even watching fish swim can help. A cat may suit a parent who is home a lot and walks with a cane. A young, strong dog may not.

A pet is also a daily anchor for someone living alone. Feeding times, walks and vet visits give the week a shape, and a dog on a leash starts conversations with neighbors. If your parent is isolated, our guide to staying connected has more ideas.

The right pet matches your parent's energy, balance and budget, not the one they had at 50.

Can a pet raise the risk of a fall?

Yes. A CDC study estimated that about 86,629 fall injuries a year in the United States were linked to dogs and cats in 2001 to 2006. The highest fracture rates were in people 75 and older.

Nearly 88% of those falls involved dogs. Common causes were tripping over a dog, being pushed or pulled by a dog, and walking a dog. About 9% came from tripping over a pet toy or food bowl. Most cat-related falls happened at home, usually from tripping over the cat.

CDC suggested awareness and obedience training for dogs. Practical steps at home:

  • Keep bowls, beds and toys out of walkways and away from the bottom of stairs.
  • Use a short, sturdy leash, and ask a trainer about calm leash walking.
  • Add night lights so a dark cat on a dark rug is visible.
  • For a big or young dog, line up a dog walker or neighbor for icy days.
  • Think about a calmer adult pet if adopting. Shelters can describe an animal's energy.

Our fall prevention guide covers the rest of the house.

Where can older adults get low-cost pet care in New Jersey?

Start with the state's low-cost spay and neuter program. It is run by the NJ Department of Health through participating veterinary hospitals.

WhoCost to spay or neuter
Owner on certain benefits$10, dog or cat
Pet adopted from eligible NJ shelter or pound$20

The $10 rate covers owners who receive food stamps (SNAP), Medicaid, General Public Assistance, rental assistance, Aid to Families with Dependent Children, Lifeline Utility Credit, Tenants Lifeline Assistance, Supplemental Security Income or Pharmaceutical Assistance to the Aged and Disabled (PAAD). Bring the benefit ID card and call a participating vet for an appointment. For the $20 adoption rate, the owner must be a New Jersey resident and have licensed the dog in town. Cats do not need a state license, though many towns require one.

Many older adults qualify for PAAD or Lifeline without realizing it means cheaper pet care too.

Dog licenses and rabies shots

New Jersey requires dogs 7 months and older to be licensed every year by the town where the owner lives. The owner must show proof of a rabies vaccine that covers at least ten months of the license year, unless a vet certifies the dog cannot be vaccinated. Towns set license fees by ordinance, and the state says they range from $1.50 to $21 per dog, plus small state fees. Ask your town clerk whether there is a senior rate.

Food and vet bills

We could not confirm a statewide pet food program for older adults. Ask your county office on aging through the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737, your local animal shelter, or dial 2-1-1, and ask whether any local pantry or program offers pet food. If money is tight overall, our guide to food and utility help may free up room in the budget.

Can my parent keep a pet in senior housing?

Often, yes. New Jersey's Pets in Housing Projects law protects residents 62 and older in senior citizen housing projects. Federally assisted senior buildings also generally cannot ban common household pets.

The New Jersey law

The law (N.J.S.A. 2A:42-103 to 113) covers buildings with three or more units, rented or owned, that are intended for and solely occupied by senior citizens. A senior citizen means someone 62 or older, plus a surviving spouse 55 or older. It does not cover licensed health care facilities, so assisted living and nursing homes set their own policies.

  • After written notice to the landlord or board, a resident may keep a dog, cat, bird, fish or other animal that is not a health or safety hazard.
  • A landlord may not arbitrarily refuse to renew a lease because of the pet. The penalty is up to $500 per offense.
  • The landlord may set reasonable written pet rules, but may not require the pet to be spayed or neutered.
  • A landlord can act if the pet breaks building or health codes, is not cared for or controlled, its waste is not cleaned up, or it is a proven continuing nuisance.

Federally assisted buildings

Federal rules (24 CFR 5.309) say owners of HUD-assisted housing for older adults or people with disabilities may not ban tenants from keeping common household pets, though they may set reasonable pet rules. Our guides to affordable senior apartments and independent living help you compare buildings. Ask for the written pet policy before signing anything.

What is the difference between a pet, a service animal and an assistance animal?

A pet is kept for company. A service animal is a dog trained to do specific tasks for a person with a disability. An assistance animal in housing is a broader category that can include emotional support animals.

Under the Americans with Disabilities Act, only dogs individually trained to do work or tasks count as service animals in stores, restaurants and other public places. Dogs whose only job is comfort do not qualify. The Department of Justice notes that the Fair Housing Act uses a broader idea of "assistance animal." Federal pet rules for assisted senior housing do not apply to animals needed as a reasonable accommodation for a disability. New Jersey's Law Against Discrimination also protects tenants with disabilities who use service or guide dogs.

If your parent needs an animal because of a disability, ask the housing provider in writing for a reasonable accommodation. Under the ADA, businesses cannot require a special ID card or training papers for a service dog, so there is no need to buy one online.

What happens to the pet if Mom moves or dies?

Plan for it now. Worry about a pet can make a hospital stay or a move much harder. A written plan and a named caregiver solve most of the worry.

  1. Name two caregivers. A first choice and a backup who have agreed and met the pet.
  2. Write a care sheet. Food, medicines, vet name and phone, habits and fears. Keep it with the emergency information sheet.
  3. Post a card. Put a note by the door and in the wallet saying a pet is home alone, with the caregiver's number. It helps if your parent is taken to the hospital.
  4. Set aside money. Talk with a lawyer about a will provision or a pet trust.
  5. Check the next home. Before a move, get the pet policy of the new building or community in writing.

New Jersey law (N.J.S.A. 3B:11-38) says a trust for the care of a domesticated animal is valid. The trust ends when no covered animal is alive, or after 21 years, whichever comes first. The money may be used only for the animal unless the trust says otherwise, and a court can reduce an amount that is far more than needed. If no trustee can serve, a court appoints one. Leftover money goes where the trust directs, or back to the owner's estate.

This is general information, not legal advice. An elder law attorney can fit a pet plan into your parent's broader estate plan. If a parent has already died and a pet needs a home, our guide on what to do when a parent dies covers the first weeks.

Where to start

For local pet food help, low-cost services or a dog walker, call your county office on aging through the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 or dial 2-1-1.

faq.q: Can my mom keep her cat in her senior apartment in New Jersey?
faq.a: In most buildings intended for and solely occupied by people 62 and older, yes. New Jersey's Pets in Housing Projects law lets her keep a domesticated animal after written notice to the landlord, subject to reasonable written rules. It does not cover assisted living or nursing homes, which set their own policies.

faq.q: Is there low-cost spay or neuter for seniors in NJ?
faq.a: Yes. The NJ Department of Health program charges $10 for a dog or cat if the owner receives benefits such as PAAD, SSI, Medicaid, SNAP or Lifeline. Show the ID card and call a participating vet.

faq.q: How do I make sure my dad's dog is cared for if he goes to the hospital?
faq.a: Name a caregiver and a backup, write a care sheet with food, medicines and the vet's number, and put a card in his wallet and by the door saying a pet is home alone with the caregiver's phone number.

faq.q: What is a pet trust in New Jersey?
faq.a: A trust that holds money for the care of a domesticated animal. New Jersey law recognizes it as valid. It ends when no covered animal is alive or after 21 years, whichever is first. A lawyer can set one up as part of an estate plan.

faq.q: Is an emotional support animal the same as a service dog?
faq.a: No. Under the ADA a service animal is a dog trained to do specific tasks for a person with a disability. Comfort alone does not qualify in public places. Housing law uses a broader assistance animal category, requested as a reasonable accommodation.

faq.q: Do pets really help older adults live longer or feel better?
faq.a: NIH says studies have found lower stress hormones and blood pressure and less loneliness with animals, but the research is young and results are mixed. The right match for a person's health and routine matters most.
